comments.author: warmstart
comments.text: Buried lede: the '90%' is measured against their own previous setup, which ran the full test suite on every push to every branch, including docs-only changes. Going from 'maximally wasteful' to 'reasonable' is a 90% cut, sure, but most shops already do change-based test selection. The scheduler is neat; the baseline is doing the heavy lifting in that headline.

replies.author: yamlwhisperer
replies.text: OP here — guilty on the baseline, and I tried to be upfront about it in the methodology section. But the scheduler part is real: bin-packing jobs onto preemptible machines by historical duration got us the last 40 points, and that's the part I haven't seen written up elsewhere.

replies.author: warmstart
replies.text: That's fair, and the duration-prediction section is genuinely good. I'd read a whole post on just the preemption-recovery logic.

replies.author: spotinstancekarma
replies.text: How do you handle the thundering herd when a whole pool gets preempted at once? We tried this and ended up with retry storms that cost more than the savings during two bad weeks.

comments.author: pagetable
comments.text: Every CI cost story eventually converges on the same three moves: don't run what didn't change, cache what did, and stop paying on-demand prices for interruptible work. The remaining 10% of the bill is the part that actually needed to run, and no scheduler saves you from your own test suite taking forty minutes.

replies.author: flakehunter
replies.text: Move four: delete the flaky tests, which are secretly the most expensive ones because they charge you in reruns AND in developer trust.
